title: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH SAUL’S CONCUBINE—And the Accusation Changed a Kingdom
paragraphs: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH SAUL’S CONCUBINE—And the Accusation Changed a Kingdom
One accusation. One furious commander. One frightened king. And a conversation about a woman that became the crack through which an entire kingdom began to change hands.
There are sentences you can take back.
And then there are sentences that change everything.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A ministry.
A family.
A kingdom.
Sometimes the sentence is shouted in anger. Sometimes whispered behind closed doors. Sometimes typed into a message and sent before wisdom has time to stop the thumb.
And sometimes it is only a question.
“Why did you do it?”
That was essentially the question Ish-bosheth put before Abner.
But this was no ordinary confrontation between two ordinary men.
One was the surviving son of Israel’s first king.
The other was the military commander whose strength was helping keep that son on the throne.
And between them stood a woman named Rizpah.
The accusation concerned sex.
But underneath it was power.
And before the conversation was finished, Abner—the man who had been strengthening Saul’s dynasty—would declare his intention to help transfer the kingdom to David.
One accusation.
One explosion.
One political rupture.
And behind all the human anger, ambition, weakness, revenge, and bloodshed, the sovereign purpose of God continued moving forward.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you have lived long enough to discover that some of the moments that changed your life did not arrive looking holy.
They arrived looking like betrayal.
Humiliation.
Failure.
Conflict.
Exposure.
A relationship breaking apart.
Someone saying something about you that you could not forget.
A door slamming shut.
A season collapsing so violently that you wondered where God had gone.
But 2 Samuel 3 confronts us with a startling truth:
Human beings can make a terrible mess without overthrowing the purposes of God.
The chapter begins with civil war.
Saul is dead, but Israel is divided. David reigns in Hebron over Judah, while Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, rules over much of Israel with Abner’s support.
Scripture describes the direction of history with devastating simplicity:
“David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.”
The transition was already happening.
Slowly.
Painfully.
God had chosen David long before David possessed the whole kingdom.
And that matters.
Because there are seasons when God’s promise seems painfully slower than your suffering.
David had been anointed, but he still had to wait.
He had survived Saul’s spear.
He had lived like a fugitive.
He had hidden in caves.
He had been hunted by the very king he once served.
And even after Saul died, David did not immediately wake up ruling a united Israel.
There was another kingdom.
Another king.
Another army.
Another struggle.
Promise did not eliminate process.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Promise does not eliminate process.
God can have a purpose for your life while your circumstances still look completely inconsistent with it.
Then comes the confrontation.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:7 reads:
“מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי”
Maddua ba'tah el-pilegesh avi?
In context:
“Why have you gone in unto my father’s concubine?”
The woman was Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
The Hebrew word used for concubine is pilegesh—פִּילֶגֶשׁ.
To modern readers, that word can sound almost incidental.
It was not.
Rizpah belonged to the household of the deceased King Saul. This accusation therefore landed in the middle of a struggle over royal authority, succession, loyalty, and power.
But here we must be careful.
Very careful.
The Bible records Ish-bosheth’s accusation.
It does not explicitly tell us that the accusation was true.
And faithful Bible teaching must never turn an accusation into a conviction simply because the accusation appears in Scripture.
Abner becomes furious.
But his response does not give us the simple courtroom answer we might expect.
He does not plainly say, “Yes, I did.”
Nor does the recorded speech give us the simple sentence, “No, I did not.”
Instead, he erupts.
“Am I a dog’s head…?”

He reminds Ish-bosheth of his loyalty to Saul’s house. He points to everything he has done to preserve the dynasty. Then he lashes out because Ish-bosheth has charged him with wrongdoing concerning this woman.
And then the conversation suddenly becomes much bigger than Rizpah.
Abner swears that he will accomplish for David what the LORD had sworn concerning David—to transfer the kingdom away from Saul’s house and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah.
Think about what just happened.
The man helping keep Ish-bosheth on the throne has essentially announced:
I am changing sides.
And Ish-bosheth says nothing.
Scripture tells us why.
He was afraid of Abner.
That detail exposes the weakness already underneath the kingdom.
Ish-bosheth wore the crown.
Abner possessed enormous practical power.
Sometimes a person can have the title and still not have the strength.
Sometimes the visible structure remains standing even after its foundations have begun collapsing.
And sometimes one confrontation merely reveals a fracture that has existed for a long time.
Abner then sends messengers to David.
“Whose is the land?”
He offers covenant and cooperation.
He tells David, in effect, that his hand will be with him to bring Israel over to David.
Soon Abner is speaking with the elders of Israel.
And here the story becomes even more revealing.
He tells them that they had wanted David as king before.
Then he urges them to act.
The accusation did not create God’s promise to David.
It did not make David God’s chosen king.
And Abner did not invent God’s purpose.
The confrontation became part of the chain of events through which an already-existing struggle moved toward a new stage.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because when something painful becomes part of a turning point in your life, you may be tempted to call the painful thing good simply because God eventually brought good through it.
Scripture gives us a better theology than that.
God does not need evil to become good before He can overrule it.
Betrayal is still betrayal.
Sin is still sin.
Falsehood is still falsehood.
Pride is still pride.
Revenge is still revenge.
Human motives can remain painfully mixed.
Yet God remains God.
Joseph understood something similar when he looked at the brothers who had sold him and declared that they had intended evil against him, but God intended it for good.
Not because their evil secretly became righteousness.
But because their evil was never powerful enough to defeat God's sovereign purpose.
And that brings this ancient royal scandal disturbingly close to home.
Because some of you are still living inside a sentence somebody spoke over you.
“You’ll never change.”
“You destroyed everything.”
“Nobody will believe you.”
“You are exactly like your father.”
“You are exactly like your mother.”
“God could never use somebody with your past.”
Maybe the accusation was false.
Maybe part of it was true.
Maybe that is what hurts most.
Maybe you actually did what they said.
Maybe there is no clever defense.
No missing context that makes you innocent.
No villain you can blame.
Maybe when you look back at the wreckage, you know your fingerprints are on it.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from reputation management.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the public image of guilty people.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend your scandal never happened.
The Gospel announces that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
There is a cross for guilty people.
There is blood for stained people.
There is mercy for ashamed people.
There is repentance for wandering people.
There is restoration for broken people.
There is a Savior for sinners.
His name is Jesus.
At Calvary, Christ did not die for an imaginary, sanitized version of you.
He died for sinners.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
And yet Scripture continues with the language of grace—being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that pats rebellion on the head and tells it to continue.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that calls us out of darkness.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday but begins changing tomorrow.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
And perhaps that is why this story should make us examine more than Abner.
It should make us examine ourselves.
What accusation would make you explode?
What subject can nobody mention without instantly touching the wound beneath your armor?
What criticism makes you disproportionately angry?
What loss are you still trying to avenge?
What relationship are you using to prove something?
What throne are you trying desperately to keep standing even though God has been exposing how fragile it really is?
And what if the thing you are protecting is not your calling but your pride?
Be honest.
Not performatively religious.
Not Sunday-morning honest.
Alone-with-God honest.
There are people who know how to lift their hands in worship while hiding entire rooms of their heart from the One they are worshiping.
We can sing about surrender and still negotiate with Jesus over the one sin we refuse to release.
We can quote Scripture publicly while privately feeding bitterness.
We can condemn somebody else’s scandal because looking at theirs keeps us from confronting ours.
But Jesus does not call us into hiding.
He calls us into light.
And light can hurt before it heals.
Abner’s story also gives us another warning.
Knowing God’s purpose is not the same as surrendering yourself to God.
Listen carefully to Abner’s own words in the chapter.
He knew that the LORD had sworn concerning David.
That is astonishing.
Abner could speak about what God intended for David while he had spent time strengthening the competing house of Saul.
A person can know biblical truth and still resist its implications.
You can know verses and still withhold your heart.
You can understand doctrine and still protect an idol.
You can know Jesus is Lord and still spend years fighting Him for control.
Knowledge about God's will is not a substitute for obedience to God.
Eventually Abner arrives in Hebron.
David prepares a feast.
Abner promises to gather Israel so that they can covenant with David.
And then Scripture says something haunting:
David sent Abner away,
“and he went in peace.”
In Hebrew:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם”
Vayelekh b'shalom.
He went in peace.
But he would not remain in peace for long.
Joab returned.
And Joab had history with Abner.
Abner had killed Joab’s brother Asahel during the earlier conflict.
Joab heard that David had received Abner and allowed him to leave.
He sent messengers after Abner and brought him back.
Then, near the gate of Hebron, Joab took Abner aside.
And killed him.
The man who had survived wars died near a city gate.
The commander who could move tribes and influence kings could not outrun the consequences of a blood-soaked world.
David publicly distances himself from the killing and mourns Abner.
And suddenly 2 Samuel 3 is no longer merely a story about an accusation involving a concubine.
It is a story crowded with wounded people.
Rizpah.
Ish-bosheth.
Abner.
David.
Joab.
Asahel.
Michal.
Paltiel.
Families.
Soldiers.
Widows.
A divided nation.
Everyone is carrying something.
Does that sound familiar?
Look closely at the people around you.
The smiling woman may be fighting grief she has never described.
The angry man may be bleeding from something that happened twenty years ago.
The person who irritates you may be carrying a battle you cannot see.
The believer sitting beside you may be one bad night away from giving up.
The person who shared this article may have shared it because they could not find the words to tell you, “This is where I am.”
We are surrounded by people carrying invisible wars.
That is why the Gospel matters so desperately.
Jesus did not enter a clean world.
He entered ours.
A world of corrupt rulers and fractured families.
Of betrayal and political maneuvering.
Of religious hypocrisy and sexual sin.
Of money and power.
Of accusations.
Of violence.
Of graves.
And into this world came the sinless Son of God.
Not another Abner.
Not another Joab.
Not another Saul.
Not merely another David.
The greater Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
David's kingdom pointed beyond itself.
Human kings die.
Human kingdoms fracture.
Human leaders fail.
Christ remains.
Jesus stood accused.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Betrayed by a friend.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And unlike every guilty human being who has ever begged for mercy, Jesus had no hidden sin requiring forgiveness.
The innocent One died for the guilty.
The King wore thorns.
The Lord of glory was nailed to wood.
And when sinful humanity appeared to have written the ending, God overturned the grave.
Jesus rose.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because every broken relationship automatically returns.
Not because repentance magically erases every earthly scar.
But because resurrection means sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over everyone who belongs to Christ.
Maybe your life has had a Saul chapter.
Maybe an Abner chapter.
Maybe a Joab chapter.
Maybe a chapter you wish could be torn completely out of the book.
Jesus already knows.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him begin changing what you thought could never change.
Stay here for a moment.
Pray.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But because sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer needed to see tonight.
Sharing a Christian article does not earn salvation.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him in faith and obedience.
But supporting and sharing faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical way to help biblical truth travel farther than it would otherwise travel.
Somebody you have never met may encounter Christ-centered truth because you refused to keep it to yourself.
Not because you need another saved post collecting digital dust.
Do you think Jesus still wants me?”
And when that moment comes, remind them:
The Gospel was made for sinners who know they need a Savior.
They are not buying God's blessing.
They are not purchasing a higher place in the Kingdom.
But their practical support can help Gospel-centered content continue being created, distributed, and placed before people who desperately need biblical truth.
Not out of guilt.
Not to prove you love God.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
“If God knew everything about me, would He still want me?”
And the answer of the cross is astonishing.
He already knows.
That is why Christ came.
Abner's accusation became entangled with the changing course of a kingdom.
But there is a greater Kingdom.
A greater King.
And a greater scandal of grace.
At the cross, the innocent Christ took the place of guilty sinners.
At the empty tomb, death discovered that it could not hold the King.

And in the Gospel, people with histories, failures, wounds, secrets, regrets, and shattered reputations are summoned not to pretend the past never happened, but to bring their entire lives beneath the lordship and mercy of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the question at the end of this story is no longer:
“Did you hear what they accused Abner of doing?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What is Jesus asking you to surrender?”
Your bitterness?
Your secret sin?
Your reputation?
Your need to be vindicated?
Your anger?
Your lust?
Your pride?
Your shame?
Your obsession with what somebody said about you?
Your desperate attempt to control how your story ends?
Bring it to Christ.
Because you were never strong enough to redeem yourself.
Neither was Abner.
Neither was David.
Neither is any of us.
We need a King who does more than rearrange earthly kingdoms.
We need a King who can forgive sinners.
Cleanse consciences.
Break chains.
Raise the dead.
And make all things new.
His name is Jesus.
Because one accusation can change the direction of an earthly kingdom.
But only one King can change the eternal destiny of a sinner who comes to Him in faith.
And maybe the line you need to remember long after you close this article is this:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life, but surrendered to Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
